questions.stem: Why can sexual reproduction help a population adapt to environmental change?

options.text: Meiosis and fertilization produce offspring with new combinations of alleles
options.why: Meiosis breaks up parental allele combinations, and fertilization combines genetic material from two gametes. The resulting variation can be acted on by natural selection.

options.text: Mitosis produces mutations in every offspring when environmental conditions change
options.why: Mitosis normally copies existing genetic information. Environmental change doesn't make every offspring acquire useful mutations.

options.text: Fertilization allows each offspring to inherit every allele from both parents
options.why: Each haploid gamete contains one allele from each parental pair, not every allele. Fertilization combines two haploid sets.

options.text: Sexual reproduction ensures that every offspring is better adapted than its parents
options.why: Variation includes neutral, harmful and beneficial combinations. Sexual reproduction doesn't guarantee improved adaptation in each offspring.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares typical male and female gametes?

options.text: Male gametes are larger because they need energy to travel to the egg
options.why: Male gametes are usually small with limited reserves. Their small size allows many to be produced.

options.text: Female gametes are smaller because the embryo receives food only after implantation
options.why: Female gametes are usually larger and contain more cytoplasm and reserves. Early development begins before implantation.

options.text: Male gametes are numerous and motile, while female gametes are larger with more reserves
options.why: Many small, motile male gametes increase the chance of reaching an egg. A larger female gamete supplies cytoplasm and reserves for early development.

options.text: Male and female gametes have equal size because both contain one chromosome set
options.why: Both are haploid, but chromosome number doesn't determine the amount of cytoplasm. Their sizes and reserves differ greatly.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the route taken by sperm from production to ejaculation?

options.text: Testis, epididymis, sperm duct, urethra
options.why: Sperm are produced in the testis, mature and are stored in the epididymis, then pass through the sperm duct and urethra.

options.text: Testis, prostate gland, epididymis, urethra
options.why: The epididymis comes directly after the testis. The prostate adds fluid later, near where the sperm duct meets the urethra.

options.text: Epididymis, testis, seminal vesicle, sperm duct
options.why: Sperm are produced before entering the epididymis. They don't pass through the seminal vesicle.

options.text: Testis, urethra, sperm duct, epididymis
options.why: This order runs backwards after the testis. The urethra is near the end of the route.

questions.stem: What directly triggers ovulation during the menstrual cycle?

options.text: A fall in progesterone caused by degeneration of the corpus luteum
options.why: That fall occurs after ovulation and leads toward menstruation. It doesn't release the egg.

options.text: A surge in LH following positive feedback from high oestradiol
options.why: Sustained high oestradiol stimulates an LH surge, and the LH surge causes the mature follicle to release the egg.

options.text: A rise in FSH following negative feedback from the endometrium
options.why: FSH supports follicle development, and the endometrium doesn't provide this feedback. The immediate trigger is the LH surge.

options.text: A rise in progesterone produced by the developing ovarian follicle
options.why: Progesterone rises mainly after ovulation because it is secreted by the corpus luteum. It maintains the endometrium.

questions.stem: A person doesn't become pregnant during a menstrual cycle. What most directly causes menstruation?

options.text: The corpus luteum degenerates, causing progesterone and oestradiol concentrations to fall
options.why: Without continued hormonal support, the endometrium breaks down and part of it is shed during menstruation.

options.text: The anterior pituitary stops producing all FSH and LH for the rest of the cycle
options.why: FSH and LH aren't permanently stopped. Their concentrations change through feedback, and FSH begins supporting another cycle.

options.text: The follicle releases an egg, physically removing the endometrium from the uterus
options.why: Ovulation occurs in an ovary and doesn't remove the uterine lining. Menstruation follows falling ovarian hormone concentrations.

options.text: The egg enters the uterus and digests the lining after failing to undergo fertilization
options.why: An unfertilized egg doesn't digest the endometrium. Hormone withdrawal causes the lining to break down.

questions.stem: Why are fertility hormones used to induce superovulation during IVF?

options.text: To make several follicles mature so several eggs can be collected
options.why: Artificial hormone treatment stimulates multiple follicles, providing several eggs that can be fertilized outside the body.

options.text: To make fertilization occur naturally in both oviducts at the same time
options.why: In IVF, fertilization occurs outside the body. The aim is to collect multiple eggs, not fertilize them in the oviducts.

options.text: To make every transferred embryo implant successfully in the endometrium
options.why: Hormone treatment can't guarantee implantation. Embryos still have to attach and develop successfully after transfer.

options.text: To convert diploid ovarian cells directly into embryos without sperm
options.why: IVF still involves eggs and sperm. Hormones stimulate follicle development rather than replacing fertilization.

questions.stem: Which event is pollination in a flowering plant?

options.text: Fusion of a male gamete with a female gamete inside an ovule
options.why: That's fertilization. It occurs after pollen has reached a compatible stigma and a pollen tube has grown.

options.text: Transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma
options.why: Pollination is a transfer event. Gamete fusion occurs later inside an ovule.

options.text: Growth of an embryo using reserves stored inside a seed
options.why: That's germination and early seedling growth. It occurs after fertilization, seed formation and dispersal.

options.text: Movement of a mature seed away from its parent plant
options.why: That's seed dispersal. Pollen is moved before fertilization, while seeds move afterward.

questions.stem: How can different maturation times of anthers and stigmas promote cross-pollination?

options.text: They prevent pollen from ever reaching a stigma on the same species
options.why: Pollen still needs to reach a compatible stigma of the same species. The timing reduces transfer within the same flower or plant.

options.text: They make pollen genetically diploid before it leaves the anther
options.why: Maturation time doesn't change pollen ploidy. Its effect is on when pollen release and stigma receptivity overlap.

options.text: They reduce overlap between pollen release and stigma receptivity on the same plant
options.why: If the male and female structures mature at different times, self-pollination becomes less likely and pollen transfer between plants is favored.

options.text: They cause the stigma to accept pollen only after a seed has formed
options.why: The stigma must receive pollen before fertilization and seed formation. Delaying it until afterward would prevent reproduction.

questions.stem: What happens during self-incompatibility in many flowering plants?

options.text: Genetic recognition prevents self-pollen from completing fertilization
options.why: The stigma or style rejects genetically incompatible self-pollen, reducing inbreeding and helping maintain variation.

options.text: Petals close permanently whenever pollen from another plant arrives
options.why: Cross-pollen is the pollen these mechanisms favor. Closing against it would reduce cross-fertilization.

options.text: The embryo rejects every allele inherited from the pollen parent
options.why: Recognition occurs before fertilization, not after an embryo forms. It affects pollen germination or pollen-tube growth.

options.text: A seed fails to germinate because it remains beside the parent plant
options.why: That's a possible consequence of poor seed dispersal. Self-incompatibility acts at the pollination and fertilization stage.

questions.stem: Why does oogenesis normally produce one large functional egg rather than four equal gametes?

options.text: Only one of the two meiotic divisions occurs in an ovarian cell
options.why: Oogenesis includes two meiotic divisions. The unequal outcome comes from cytokinesis, not from omitting meiosis.

options.text: Unequal cytokinesis gives most of the cytoplasm to one cell
options.why: The other haploid products become small polar bodies, while one egg retains the cytoplasm and reserves needed for early development.

options.text: Three haploid products fuse together before the egg is released
options.why: The products don't fuse. The smaller cells are polar bodies produced by unequal divisions.

options.text: The primary oocyte destroys three chromosome sets during meiosis
options.why: Chromosomes are separated into haploid products rather than destroyed. Cytoplasm is distributed unequally.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly states the roles of the acrosome and cortical reactions?

options.text: The acrosome reaction blocks sperm, while the cortical reaction attracts another sperm
options.why: The roles run in the opposite direction. The acrosome helps the first sperm enter, and the cortical reaction blocks others.

options.text: The acrosome reaction starts implantation, while the cortical reaction forms the placenta
options.why: Both reactions occur at fertilization around the egg. Implantation and placental development happen later in the uterus.

options.text: The acrosome reaction digests the egg membrane, while the cortical reaction destroys the sperm nucleus
options.why: Acrosomal enzymes help penetrate the zona pellucida, not the egg membrane itself. The cortical reaction doesn't destroy the sperm nucleus.

options.text: The acrosome reaction permits zona penetration, while the cortical reaction prevents polyspermy
options.why: Acrosomal enzymes help one sperm cross the zona pellucida. Cortical granules then modify the zona so additional sperm can't enter.

questions.stem: What does a positive home pregnancy test detect?

options.text: Progesterone released into urine by the corpus luteum
options.why: Standard tests detect hCG rather than progesterone. Progesterone can be present during non-pregnant menstrual cycles.

options.text: A fetal blood cell that has crossed directly into the urine
options.why: Pregnancy tests detect a soluble hormone, not fetal cells. Fetal and maternal blood normally remain separate.

options.text: hCG bound by specific monoclonal antibodies in the test
options.why: The embryo or developing placenta secretes hCG. Antibodies in the test bind it and produce a visible test line.

options.text: LH remaining in the blood after the ovulation surge
options.why: LH triggers ovulation but isn't the pregnancy marker measured by the test. The marker is hCG.

questions.stem: Which exchange normally occurs across the placenta?

options.text: Maternal red blood cells enter fetal capillaries to deliver oxygen
options.why: Whole maternal red blood cells normally remain in the maternal circulation. Oxygen crosses between the two blood supplies.

options.text: Fetal urea enters maternal blood, while oxygen enters fetal blood
options.why: The fetus transfers nitrogenous waste toward the mother and receives oxygen. Placental villi provide a large exchange surface.

options.text: Fetal carbon dioxide enters the uterus and leaves through the cervix
options.why: Carbon dioxide crosses into maternal blood and is removed by the mother's lungs. It doesn't leave through the cervix.

options.text: Maternal and fetal blood mix freely inside the placental villi
options.why: The two circulations normally remain separate. Materials cross the placental barrier between them.

questions.stem: Why did randomized controlled trials change the conclusion that HRT protects against coronary heart disease?

options.text: They showed that every person taking HRT developed coronary heart disease
options.why: The trials found a small increase in risk, not disease in every participant. Risk describes a probability.

options.text: They removed all biological variation between every treatment and control participant
options.why: Randomization balances confounding variables between groups on average. It doesn't make individual participants biologically identical.

options.text: They proved socioeconomic status has no relationship with coronary heart disease
options.why: Socioeconomic status was an important confounder in the earlier studies. The trials didn't show that its relationship disappeared.

options.text: Random allocation reduced confounding and revealed a small increase in risk with HRT
options.why: Earlier HRT users tended to have higher socioeconomic status, which was associated with lower disease risk. Randomized evidence didn't support a protective causal effect.
